summary: Swiss food giant Nestlé aggressively marketed infant formula over breastfeeding in poor countries from the 1950s to the 1980s, where unsafe water and over-dilution led to mass infant malnutrition and death.
keywords: International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes

evidence.note: Henri Nestle completes his powdered milk-and-grain formula by 1867
1960s-70s global expansion of formula sales into poorer nations begins
company-employed mothercraft nurses dressed as medical staff push formula
ad campaigns shaming mothers about inadequate breast milk, e.g. Lactogen slogan
Malawi households lacking running water and kitchens to prepare formula safely
Dr Morley's study of breastfeeding in rural Nigerian villages
Jamaican mother over-diluting formula; babies severely malnourished
Ivory Coast infant starving on formula; Nestle cuts free supply to hospitals
1981 World Health Assembly adopts marketing code for breast milk substitutes
2018 Changing Markets report and WHA breastfeeding resolution fight

notes: Opening ~8 min on 18th-century wet nursing is background, not Nestle's own story, so covered_span starts at the 1867 formula. Roles: primary is a company; business-executive applies only to secondary Henri Nestle, whom the story calls not a bastard. Setting spans many countries (also CD, UG, SG, PE, CR, ID, CH); top six kept by airtime of harm.
